```{r analysis, include=FALSE}
analysis <- new.env()
source(file.path(report_dir, "correlate-climate-spatial-latents.R"), local = analysis)
results <- analysis$correlation_summary
fitted <- results[results$cell_set == "fitted", ]
common <- results[results$cell_set == "common", ]
map_names <- unlist(lapply(1:3, function(a) sprintf(
  "atlas%d-spatial-latents-posterior-%s.png", a, c("mean", "sd"))))
if (!all(file.exists(file.path(report_dir, map_names)))) {
  source(file.path(report_dir, "plot-spatial-latents.R"), local = new.env())
}
show_png <- function(name) knitr::include_graphics(file.path(report_dir, name), rel_path = FALSE)
fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
correlation_table <- function(atlas, cell_set = "fitted") {
  d <- results[results$atlas == atlas & results$cell_set == cell_set, ]
  d <- d[order(match(d$climate, c("Temperature", "Precipitation")), d$factor), ]
  data.frame(Climate = d$climate, Factor = d$factor,
    `Mean-map r` = fmt(d$mean_map_r), `Draw median r` = fmt(d$median_r),
    `95% draw interval` = paste0("[", fmt(d$lower_r), ", ", fmt(d$upper_r), "]"),
    `R-hat` = fmt(d$rhat), `Bulk ESS` = round(d$ess_bulk),
    `Tail ESS` = round(d$ess_tail), check.names = FALSE)
}
diagnostics <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("fitted", "common"), function(cs) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(a) {
    d <- results[results$atlas == a & results$cell_set == cs, ]
    data.frame(Cells = cs, Atlas = a, `N cells` = unique(d$n_cells),
      `R-hat >= 1.1 (of 10)` = sum(d$rhat >= 1.1),
      `Median R-hat` = fmt(median(d$rhat)), `Maximum R-hat` = fmt(max(d$rhat)),
      `Minimum bulk ESS` = round(min(d$ess_bulk)), check.names = FALSE)
  }))
}))
strongest <- fitted[which.max(abs(fitted$mean_map_r)), ]
```

## Question and sample

This report shows all five spatial latent factors from each of the three
**`2026-11-02_06-55-21`** Hmsc models. It also examines how their spatial patterns
overlap with breeding-season temperature and precipitation.

We use all four chains and all 250 retained draws per chain, giving **1,000
draws per atlas**. The maps and primary correlations use every fitted cell:
1,747 in the 1970s, 1,821 in the 1990s, and 1,875 in the 2010s. A separate
correlation analysis uses the same **1,697 cells shared by all three atlases**.
The latter keeps spatial coverage consistent, although each atlas retains its
own climate measurements and fitted model.

**The derived correlations exhibit substantial chain disagreement.** For the
fitted-cell analysis, `r sum(fitted$rhat >= 1.1)` of 30 climate–factor correlations
have rank-normalised R-hat at least 1.1. We therefore present these as descriptive
diagnostics, not reliable evidence that particular factors are associated with
climate. The pooled intervals below describe the saved draws and should not be
treated as well-converged posterior credible intervals.

## What the spatial factors represent

The model's linear predictor contains a fixed environmental contribution and
a spatial contribution:

\[
L = X\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\eta}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}.
\]

Each column of **Eta** is a spatial latent-factor coordinate at the modelled
cells. **Lambda** describes how species load onto those factors. The maps below
show Eta itself, not the combined species-specific spatial contribution
\(\boldsymbol{\eta}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\).

We retain the saved within-model alignment used during posterior import.
Individual factor signs, orientation, and ordering are arbitrary. Factor 1 in
Atlas 1 is not necessarily the counterpart of factor 1 in another atlas.
Flipping a factor's sign also flips its correlation sign without changing the
model when its loadings are flipped correspondingly. Correlations with individual
factors additionally depend on the chosen orientation of the latent-factor basis.

## Spatial patterns and uncertainty

For each cell and factor, we calculate the arithmetic mean and sample SD across
all 1,000 saved draws. Means share one zero-centred colour scale across all maps;
SDs share one sequential scale. No value ranges are clipped. The white-centred
mean scale can make small values look faint, especially beside larger values
elsewhere.

Maps use the stored fitted coordinates, transformed from EPSG:23032 to
longitude/latitude. Latent rows are linked to cells through `Pi` and `dfPi`, and
cell locations are checked against the local atlas grid. Bornholm appears in
each inset. Every fitted cell is included.

SD is uncertainty conditional on the saved factor alignment. It is not a
convergence diagnostic. Pooled mean and SD maps can conceal disagreement between
chains, including possible unresolved orientation differences.

## Climate correlations

### Calculation and interpretation

We calculate **Pearson correlations across cells** between each climate variable
and each of the five spatial factors, separately within each atlas. Climate
values come directly from the fitted model's `XData`, aligned to the same rows
as Eta. They were standardised before fitting; Pearson correlation is unchanged
by centring and positive rescaling, so it is the same correlation as for the
corresponding original-unit climate values on these cells.

Two summaries answer related but different questions:

- **Mean-map correlation:** correlate climate with the posterior mean Eta at
  each cell. This measures overlap with the spatial pattern visible in the map.
- **Draw-level correlation:** correlate climate with Eta separately for every
  posterior draw, then summarise the 1,000 correlations. This includes uncertainty
  in Eta, conditional on the fitted model and saved alignment.

The correlation of a mean map need not equal the mean or median correlation
across draws, because correlation is a nonlinear standardised statistic. A
small mean-map amplitude also does not imply a small correlation.

We report medians and equal-tail 2.5–97.5% intervals of the saved draw-level
correlations, together with chain diagnostics. Climate values and the chosen
cell sets are held fixed. Measurement error in climate, model misspecification,
and alternative factor alignments are not propagated.

We do **not** run ordinary `cor.test` significance tests: neighbouring cells
are spatially dependent and would not constitute independent replicates for
those tests. The draw intervals quantify model-based uncertainty, subject to
convergence; they do not establish causal effects or independent-sample
significance. These are marginal correlations, without adjustment for the other
climate variable or other predictors.

```

The largest absolute mean-map correlation among these 30 comparisons is for
**`r strongest$climate`, Atlas `r strongest$atlas`, factor `r strongest$factor`**:
mean-map r = **`r fmt(strongest$mean_map_r)`**. The draw-level median is
`r fmt(strongest$median_r)`, with a pooled-draw interval of
[`r fmt(strongest$lower_r)`, `r fmt(strongest$upper_r)`] and R-hat
`r fmt(strongest$rhat)`. This illustrates why a map correlation and a
well-estimated posterior association are different claims. We do not label
this or the other comparisons statistically supported.

### Shared-cell sensitivity analysis

The following analysis restricts every atlas to the same 1,697 cells, ordered
by cell identity. It checks sensitivity to changing spatial coverage, without
refitting the models. Factors remain defined within their original fitted model.

```{r common-correlations, fig.cap="Climate–factor correlations evaluated on the same 1,697 cells in all three atlases. This does not make factor numbers comparable between atlases."}
show_png("climate-spatial-latent-correlations-common.png")
```

```{r common-tables, results='asis'}
for (atlas in 1:3) {
  cat("\n\n#### Atlas ", atlas, " on shared cells\n\n", sep = "")
  print(knitr::kable(correlation_table(atlas, "common"),
                     caption = paste("Atlas", atlas, ": 1,697 shared cells.")))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

For matched atlas–climate–factor comparisons, restricting to the common cells
changes the mean-map correlations by at most
**`r fmt(max(abs(fitted$mean_map_r - common$mean_map_r)))`** and the draw medians
by at most **`r fmt(max(abs(fitted$median_r - common$median_r)))`**.
This is a coverage sensitivity check, not a test of temporal change.

## All environmental predictors and the combined spatial effect

The individual-factor comparisons above depend on the saved latent basis.
To ask whether overlap is pervasive across predictors, we also correlate all
ten original environmental variables with the **combined spatial contribution
for each species**, Eta × Lambda. This is an inferred model component, not an
independently measured environmental field. No spatially detrended climate
predictors are used in this comparison.

For every draw, we multiply that draw's Eta and Lambda, then calculate each
predictor's Pearson correlation with the resulting spatial effect across the
same 1,697 shared cells. We retain all 155 matched species and all 1,000 draws
per atlas. Unlike individual-factor correlations, the combined effect is
unchanged by compensating rotations, permutations, or sign changes of the
factors and loadings. We verify the efficient covariance calculation against
direct correlations of Eta × Lambda for selected draws.

### Distribution across species

Each point below is one species' median draw-level correlation. Violin and
boxplot widths describe variation **among species**, not posterior uncertainty
for those estimates. A mixture of positive and negative correlations can
produce a mean close to zero while still involving substantial overlap.

```{r environment-combined-distributions}
show_png("environment-spatial-effect-correlations.png")
```

### Strength of overlap and uncertainty

Within each draw, we take the absolute correlations and calculate their median
across all species. We then show the median and 2.5–97.5% interval of these
draw-level community summaries. Absolute values prevent opposite species
directions from cancelling. The species set is fixed; we do not bootstrap
species or treat posterior draws as independent cell observations.

```{r environment-combined-strength}
show_png("environment-spatial-effect-correlation-strength.png")
```

```{r environment-combined-tables,results='asis'}
for(a in 1:3) {
  d <- combined_strength[combined_strength$atlas==a,]
  checks <- combined$effect_diagnostic_summary
  checks <- checks[checks$atlas==a,]
  stopifnot(identical(d$variable,checks$variable))
  tab <- data.frame(Predictor=unname(combined$variable_labels[d$variable]),
    `Median |r|`=fmt(d$estimate),
    `95% draw interval`=paste0("[",fmt(d$lower),", ",fmt(d$upper),"]"),
    `Community R-hat`=fmt(d$rhat),`Community bulk ESS`=round(d$ess_bulk),
    `Species r R-hat >= 1.1 (of 155)`=checks$n_species_rhat_ge_1_1,
    check.names=FALSE)
  cat("\n\n### Atlas ",a," combined spatial effects\n\n",sep="")
  print(knitr::kable(tab));cat("\n\n")
}
```

Atlas 3 precipitation has the largest community median absolute correlation
in this summary: **`r fmt(combined_strength$estimate[combined_strength$atlas==3 & combined_strength$variable=='prec_breeding'])`**.
Overlap varies among predictors and species; it is not equally pronounced
everywhere. No formal test of changing correlations between atlases is performed.

These diagnostics are different from the previously examined **posterior
trade-off between Beta and the spatial contribution**. The new plots describe
correlation across cells within draws, whereas the trade-off describes how
fixed and spatial components compensate as parameters vary across draws.
Small cross-cell correlations do not establish that coefficients are well
identified, and larger values do not quantify coefficient bias or prove
spatial confounding. Community and species-level chain diagnostics are
reported separately because they can differ substantially. Pooled intervals
remain conditional on the model and adequacy of sampling.

## Chain agreement and limits on inference

We preserve chain identities for every draw-level correlation and compute
rank-normalised split/folded R-hat, bulk ESS, tail ESS, and Monte Carlo SE of
the mean using the `posterior` package. R-hat assesses chain agreement; ESS
describes sampling efficiency rather than the number of cells. The tables
below use 1.1 as a flag for conspicuous disagreement, not as a criterion that
all smaller values are satisfactory. See the official documentation for
[R-hat](https://mc-stan.org/posterior/reference/rhat.html) and
[bulk ESS](https://mc-stan.org/posterior/reference/ess_bulk.html).

```{r diagnostic-summary}
knitr::kable(diagnostics, caption = "Diagnostics of the derived climate–factor correlations.")
```

```{r chain-comparison, fig.cap="Chain-specific mean correlations on fitted cells. Separation among chains shows disagreement hidden by pooled summaries; factor numbers are categorical within-atlas labels."}
show_png("climate-spatial-latent-correlations-chains.png")
```

The maximum fitted-cell correlation R-hat is **`r fmt(max(fitted$rhat))`**.
Diagnostics of Eta or Gamma individually do not guarantee convergence of
these derived correlations. Chain disagreement could reflect slow sampling,
unresolved factor alignment, or both. These results do not by themselves
distinguish those mechanisms.

Individual-factor correlations are also not a complete diagnostic of the
previously observed trade-off between Beta and space. Such trade-offs involve
the species-specific **combined** spatial effect, \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\), including
its average level and its projections onto the environmental predictors.
Weak correlations for individual factors would not rule out that problem;
strong correlations would not quantify how much of a species' fitted response
has been assigned to climate instead of space.

A useful subsequent analysis would therefore check quantities invariant to
joint factor rotations, such as the combined species-specific spatial effects,
alongside draw-level VP and their chain diagnostics. No new fitting or VP
change tests have been performed here.

## Reproducibility and validation

Knitting this report recomputes all climate–factor and environment–combined-effect
correlations, diagnostics, and five correlation PNGs. Existing map PNGs are embedded; if any are missing,
the map script regenerates the full set. To regenerate maps explicitly and
render the report from the repository root:

```{r reproduce, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
source("scripts/5-vis/spatial-latents/plot-spatial-latents.R")
rmarkdown::render("scripts/5-vis/spatial-latents/spatial-latents.Rmd")
```

The correlation script retains `correlation_summary`, `correlation_draws`, and
`correlation_chains` in memory for further inspection. It verifies model sizes,
site alignment, finite values, all 1,000 draws, the common-cell intersection,
and vectorised calculations against direct correlations for a selected draw
for every climate–factor combination. There are 60 summaries and 60,000
draw-level correlations across the two cell sets. All generated plots are PNGs;
the rendered HTML embeds them and can be read without separate image files.

The additional `correlate-environment-spatial-effect.R` script retains
`effect_draws`, `effect_species_summary`, `effect_community_summary`, and
`effect_diagnostic_summary` in memory. It checks all ten predictors, matched
species/site indexing, valid spatial-effect variances, finite correlations,
direct matrix-product agreement, and invariance to factor permutation/sign
changes. It creates two additional PNGs and does not modify fitted models.
